newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel says Arabs trying to topple its government.
newsitem.headline: Israel says Arabs trying to topple its government.

text.p: Israel slammed a threat by Arab states to backtrack on steps towards normal ties with it as "diplomatic violence" on Monday, accusing the Arabs of trying to topple the Israeli government.
"The peace process doesn't tolerate and will not tolerate an atmosphere of violence -- not on the ground and not in diplomatic violence," Foreign Minister David Levy told reporters.

He said an Arab League call for its members to suspend normalisation was part of a bid to bring down Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government that began when it came to power nine months ago.

On Sunday, Arab League foreign ministers recommended member states suspend steps toward normal relations with Israel and renew an Arab boycott over a Jewish settlement going up on a hill in Arab East Jerusalem.

In a 12th straight day of West Bank clashes spurred by the settlement building, Israeli troops firing rubber bullets shot and wounded two Palestinians during a clash near Jenin with about 200 protesters who were throwing stones.

In a move assailed by human rights activists as collective punishment, Israel flattened the West Bank family apartment of a Palestinian suicide bomber who killed three Israeli women in a Tel Aviv cafe on March 21.
The groundbreaking for the settlement this month and the suicide attack, coupled with daily clashes, have plunged Israeli-Arab relations to another low point in five years of peacemaking.
In Jerusalem, Levy said Middle East peace moves must not be held hostage to violence or a halt in normalisation.

"Israel is going with a peace process from its desire and free choice...Obviously it won't take on itself things that run contrary to its interests or its policy as a result of pressure or violence," he said.

Netanyahu's communications chief David Bar-Illan assailed the threat to restore the Arab boycott, telling Reuters: "It is a reversion to hostile acts rather than an effort to sit around the table and settle our differences through negotiations."
Israel's central bank governor Jacob Frenkel declined comment on the revived threat but termed the end of the Arab boycott one of the main benefits which Israel had reaped from peace efforts.

Arab foreign ministers said the league draft would put an end to the tentative gestures of Arab countries such as Morocco, Tunisia, Oman and Qatar towards Israel since the Jewish state's first agreement with the Palestinians in 1993.
"It was an important meeting in which we discussed in detail the Israeli breaching of what has been agreed upon," President Yasser Arafat said in the Palestinian-ruled Gaza Strip.
"And the decision was clear and obvious -- to put on the correct line the peace process," he told reporters.
Palestinians complain the settlement of 6,500 houses for Jews pre-empts the results of final peace talks yet to come on the status of East Jerusalem, which each side claims as its own.
Egypt and Jordan, the two states which could have the greatest impact, appeared to be exempt from the Arab action.

"This decision does not apply to Jordan and Egypt. We have a peace treaty. There is an international obligation to respect the treaty," Jordan's Ambassador to Israel Omar Rifai said in a speech to the Begin-Sadat Centre for Strategic Studies at Bar-Ilan University near Tel Aviv.

"The Jordanian opinion is that Jerusalem is an issue which has to be dealt with in the final-status talks and dealt with not unilaterally by informing the Palestinians of a decision but by sitting down and negotiating with the Palestinains on any and all issues concerning Jerusalem," he said.
